item.stem: A block slides down a straight, frictionless ramp that rises toward the right. Air resistance is negligible. Which description gives a complete, correct free-body diagram for the block, with every arrow starting at the dot representing the block?

choices.choice_text: Four arrows: gravitational force vertically downward, normal force perpendicular to the ramp, and the two components of gravitational force parallel and perpendicular to the ramp.
choices.rationale: Component double-counting: Drawing gravitational force and its components counts the same interaction twice. Components represent a force along chosen axes, not additional forces. Fix: Draw each interaction once, and resolve components separately from the free-body diagram.

choices.choice_text: Two arrows: gravitational force vertically downward and normal force perpendicular to the ramp, away from its surface.
choices.rationale: Earth exerts a downward gravitational force, and the frictionless ramp exerts a normal force perpendicular to its surface. These are the only forces on the block; components are not drawn as additional force arrows.

choices.choice_text: Two arrows: gravitational force vertically downward and normal force vertically upward.
choices.rationale: Always-up normal force misconception: The normal force is perpendicular to the contact surface, not necessarily vertical. A vertical arrow is not perpendicular to this inclined ramp. Fix: Identify the surface orientation, then draw the normal force perpendicular to it.

choices.choice_text: Three arrows: gravitational force vertically downward, normal force perpendicular to the ramp, and an additional force of motion directed down the ramp.
choices.rationale: Motion-requires-a-force misconception: The block's motion does not create an additional force. A force arrow must represent an interaction with another object, not the block's velocity. Fix: Name the object exerting each proposed force before drawing its arrow.

object.defect: The ramp's tilt direction and the block's sliding direction are irrelevant to the free-body diagram; no material defect.

flags: defect: The ramp's tilt direction and the block's sliding direction are irrelevant to the free-body diagram; no material defect.

item.stem: A small piece of ice slides upward along the curved inside surface of a bowl. At its present position, the surface rises toward the left at 30° above horizontal. The contact is frictionless, and air resistance is negligible. Which set of arrows should be drawn from the ice's dot to make its complete free-body diagram?

choices.choice_text: Four arrows: gravitational force vertically downward, normal force perpendicular to the local surface, and gravitational force components parallel and perpendicular to that surface.
choices.rationale: Component double-counting: Including gravity together with its components represents the same interaction more than once. Components describe a force along selected axes; they are not separate interactions. Fix: Draw gravity once, then resolve its components outside the free-body diagram.

choices.choice_text: Two arrows: gravitational force vertically downward and normal force vertically upward.
choices.rationale: Always-up normal force misconception: A normal force follows the perpendicular to the contact surface, not a fixed upward direction. Here, a vertical arrow is not perpendicular to the tilted surface. Fix: Locate the contact surface and draw its outward perpendicular.

choices.choice_text: Two arrows: gravitational force vertically downward and normal force perpendicular to the local surface, pointing upward and rightward.
choices.rationale: The ice interacts with Earth through gravity and with the bowl through a normal force directed away from the local surface. With friction and air resistance absent, these two arrows represent all forces acting on the ice.

choices.choice_text: Three arrows: gravitational force vertically downward, normal force perpendicular to the local surface, and a force of motion directed upward along the surface.
choices.rationale: Motion-requires-a-force misconception: Moving upward does not give the ice an additional force of motion. That proposed arrow describes its motion rather than an interaction with another object. Fix: Identify an interacting object for every proposed force arrow.

item.stem: A child gives a sled a brief shove, then lets go. The sled coasts up an icy, frictionless hillside that rises toward the left at 25° above horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. While the sled is still moving up the hill after the shove has ended, which description gives its complete, correct free-body diagram, with every arrow starting at the sled's dot?

choices.choice_text: Four arrows: gravitational force vertically downward, normal force perpendicular to the hillside, and the components of gravitational force along and perpendicular to the hillside.
choices.rationale: Component double-counting: the two components are just gravitational force expressed along tilted axes, not additional interactions. Drawing both the force and its components counts Earth's pull twice. Fix: Draw each interaction once, then resolve components only in your separate Newton's law equations.

choices.choice_text: Two arrows: gravitational force vertically downward and normal force perpendicular to the hillside, pointing away from the snow surface.
choices.rationale: Only two objects interact with the sled: Earth pulls it straight down, and the frictionless snow surface pushes perpendicular to itself, away from the surface. The shove has ended, and components of gravity are not separate forces, so these are the only arrows.

choices.choice_text: Two arrows: gravitational force vertically downward and normal force vertically upward.
choices.rationale: Always-up normal force misconception: a normal force is perpendicular to the contact surface, not automatically vertical. On a 25° slope, a vertical arrow is not perpendicular to the snow. Fix: Identify the contact surface's tilt, then draw the normal force perpendicular to that surface.

choices.choice_text: Three arrows: gravitational force vertically downward, normal force perpendicular to the hillside, and a force from the shove directed up the hill.
choices.rationale: Motion-requires-a-force misconception: the sled moves uphill because of its existing velocity, not because the shove still acts. The child is no longer touching the sled, so no push force exists. Fix: For each proposed arrow, name the object currently exerting that force on the sled.

item.stem: A plastic slider travels upward along the inner surface of a frictionless vertical loop, remaining in contact with it. At the slider’s location on the upper-right part of the loop, the surface slopes downward toward the right at 40° to the horizontal. Ignore air resistance. Which description specifies the slider’s complete free-body diagram, with all arrows beginning at its dot?

choices.choice_text: Four arrows: gravity straight downward, the normal force perpendicular to the surface into the loop’s interior, and gravity’s components parallel and perpendicular to the surface.
choices.rationale: Component double-counting: Including gravity together with its two components represents the same gravitational interaction twice. Components are an alternative representation, not additional forces. Fix: Draw gravity once, then resolve its components outside the free-body diagram.

choices.choice_text: Two arrows: gravity straight downward and the normal force straight upward.
choices.rationale: Always-up normal force misconception: A normal force follows the perpendicular to the contact surface, not a fixed upward direction. Here, a vertical arrow is not perpendicular to the surface. Fix: Sketch the local surface orientation and mark its inward perpendicular before drawing the normal force.

choices.choice_text: Three arrows: gravity straight downward, the normal force perpendicular to the surface into the loop’s interior, and a force of motion upward along the surface.
choices.rationale: Motion-requires-a-force misconception: Upward motion does not supply another interaction acting on the slider. Its direction of travel is not an extra force. Fix: Identify an external object responsible for each proposed force arrow.

choices.choice_text: Two arrows: gravity straight downward and the normal force perpendicular to the surface, pointing downward and left into the loop’s interior.
choices.rationale: The slider interacts with Earth and the loop: Earth supplies gravity, and the frictionless surface supplies a perpendicular normal force into the loop’s interior. Each interaction appears once, without additional component arrows.

object.defect: Minor wording issue: a slider on the upper-right part of a loop that is still moving "upward" would be going counterclockwise, so on the incline it would be moving up-left, while the stem describes the surface as "sloping downward toward the right." This does not change the free-body diagram. Only gravity (straight down) and the normal force act. The normal force is perpendicular to the surface and points toward the center, which is down and to the left. Choice A double-counts gravity by adding its components, B gives the wrong direction for the normal force, and C adds a fictitious force of motion.

item.stem: A box is pulled by a rope across a frictionless horizontal floor. In case 1, the rope is horizontal and pulls rightward. In case 2, the rope pulls upward and rightward at an angle above horizontal. The box remains in contact with the floor in both cases, and air resistance is negligible. Comparing complete free-body diagrams for the box, how should the number of force arrows and the representation of the rope’s force change?

choices.choice_text: Three arrows in case 1 and five in case 2; the angled tension arrow is drawn along with its horizontal and vertical components.
choices.rationale: This is the force-and-components double-counting error. The components describe the same rope force, so drawing them alongside the tension arrow counts that interaction more than once. Fix: Draw the tension once along the rope and resolve components separately.

choices.choice_text: Three arrows in case 1 and four in case 2; the angled tension arrow is replaced by horizontal and vertical component arrows.
choices.rationale: This is the components-as-forces error. A free-body diagram shows the actual rope force along the rope, rather than replacing it with component arrows. Fix: Replace the two component arrows with one arrow along the rope.

choices.choice_text: Three arrows in each case; the rope’s force changes from rightward to upward and rightward.
choices.rationale: The box interacts with Earth, the floor, and the rope, so each diagram contains gravitational, normal, and tension forces. Tilting the rope changes the tension arrow’s direction, not the number of forces.

choices.choice_text: Four arrows in each case, including a separate net-force arrow; the rope’s force changes from rightward to upward and rightward.
choices.rationale: This is the net-force-as-an-extra-force error. Net force is the vector sum of the forces already shown, not an additional interaction with the box. Fix: Match each force arrow to an interaction and remove the separate net-force arrow.

item.stem: A collar slides along a vertical pole with negligible friction. A rigid rod presses on the collar, which stays in contact with the pole. In arrangement 1, the rod’s force points leftward and downward at 30° below horizontal. In arrangement 2, its force points horizontally leftward. Ignore air resistance. Which description gives the complete free-body diagrams for the collar, with every arrow starting at the collar’s dot?

choices.choice_text: Both diagrams contain three arrows; the rod-force arrow points leftward and downward in arrangement 1 and directly leftward in arrangement 2.
choices.rationale: Each diagram shows one gravitational force from Earth, one normal force from the pole, and one applied force from the rod. Changing the rod’s direction rotates its force arrow without adding or removing an interaction.

choices.choice_text: Arrangement 1 contains five arrows and arrangement 2 contains three; the angled rod-force arrow appears together with its horizontal and vertical components.
choices.rationale: The force-and-components double-counting error treats parts of one force as additional interactions. The component arrows represent the same push already shown by the angled arrow. Fix: Keep one arrow for the rod’s push and resolve its components outside the diagram.

choices.choice_text: Arrangement 1 contains four arrows and arrangement 2 contains three; horizontal and vertical component arrows replace the angled rod-force arrow.
choices.rationale: The components-as-forces error substitutes mathematical components for the actual applied force. The free-body diagram must represent the rod’s push with one arrow in its actual direction. Fix: Replace the component arrows with a single arrow pointing along the applied push.

choices.choice_text: Both diagrams contain four arrows, including an additional net-force arrow; the rod-force arrow changes from leftward and downward to directly leftward.
choices.rationale: The net-force-as-an-extra-force error adds the result of combining forces as though it were another interaction. A net-force arrow does not belong alongside the individual forces in a free-body diagram. Fix: Identify the source of each force and delete any separate net-force arrow.

choices.rationale: This is the force-and-components double-counting error. Adding component arrows alongside the pushrod-force arrow represents the same interaction more than once. Fix: Keep one pushrod-force arrow and resolve its components outside the free-body diagram.

choices.choice_text: Trial 1 has three arrows and trial 2 has four; trial 2 replaces the pushrod-force arrow with components parallel and perpendicular to the ramp.
choices.rationale: This is the components-as-forces error. The diagram must show the actual pushrod force, not substitute two component arrows for that force. Fix: Replace the component arrows with one arrow in the pushrod force’s actual direction.

choices.choice_text: Each diagram has three arrows; the pushrod-force arrow changes from parallel to the ramp to tilted toward its surface.
choices.rationale: Earth, the ramp, and the pushrod exert gravitational, normal, and applied forces on the puck. Changing the pushrod’s direction rotates its force arrow without adding another interaction.

choices.choice_text: Each diagram has four arrows, including a separate net-force arrow; the pushrod-force arrow changes from parallel to the ramp to tilted toward its surface.
choices.rationale: This is the net-force-as-an-extra-force error. The net force combines the forces acting on the puck; it is not another interaction. Fix: Identify the interaction behind each arrow and delete any separate net-force arrow.

object.defect: The ramp is frictionless, so the puck experiences exactly three forces in both trials: gravity, the normal force, and the pushrod force. A free-body diagram shows only actual forces, with no components and no net-force arrow. That rules out A, B, and D. In trial 2 only the direction of the pushrod arrow changes. Choice C matches this.

item.stem: A steel puck slides down a frictionless inclined ramp while a rigid pushrod pushes on it. During trial 1, the pushrod’s force points directly down the ramp, parallel to its surface. During trial 2, that force points 30° away from the downhill direction, tilted toward the ramp’s surface. The puck maintains contact with the ramp, and air resistance can be ignored. With all arrows starting at the puck’s dot, which description correctly compares its complete free-body diagrams?
